summary: This RFC updates RFC 5043 and RFC 5044 by extending MPA negotiation for RDMA connection establishment. One enhancement enables peer-to-peer connection establishment, and another adds an option for standardized connection setup.

eli5.summary: Two computers that share memory directly need a better handshake. This adds ways for them to set up more flexibly.

what is ird and ord in rdma
what is an rtr indication in mpa
subtitle: A better opening handshake for RDMA over TCP and SCTP, with peer-to-peer setup and standard read-queue negotiation.

tldr.problem: RDMA connection setup over MPA/TCP assumes a client that sends the first message, which does not suit peer-to-peer applications, and it leaves the RDMA Read queue sizes (IRD and ORD) to each upper-layer protocol to negotiate in its own way.
tldr.mechanism: A new S bit in the MPA Request and Reply Frames says that the Private Data starts with a 32-bit block holding IRD, ORD and four control flags. The block negotiates the queue depths and which zero-length message the initiator sends as a Ready to Receive (RTR) indication. SCTP gets three matching new function codes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6581 updates RFC 5043 and RFC 5044. Enhanced setup is optional and falls back to the older exchange, but an unenhanced responder closes the TCP connection when it sees an enhanced request.

facts.label: Enhanced data size
facts.value: 32 bits at the start of Private Data

today: RFC 6581 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5043 and RFC 5044, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.content:
When the Remote Direct Data Placement (RDDP) protocols run over TCP, they use MPA (Marker PDU Aligned Framing, RFC 5044) both to set up the connection and to add markers to the TCP stream. In the usual model, a passive side listens, an active side asks to connect with some RDMA parameters and private application data, and the passive side decides whether to accept.

The RFC names two limits. MPA only supports a client-server model, which forces peer-to-peer applications to act as if they had a client and a server. And some RDMA-layer parameters are left to each upper layer protocol (ULP) to negotiate. The document therefore has two goals: support a peer-to-peer model for connection setup, and add negotiation of the RDMA Read queue size for both sides.

It updates both RFC 5043 (the SCTP adaptation) and RFC 5044 (the MPA specification for TCP).
sections.eli5: Today the computer that calls always has to talk first, like a phone call where the caller must speak before anyone else can. This RFC lets two equals set up the call fairly, and agree on the rules first.

sections.title: Why the Old Handshake Falls Short
sections.content:
An RDMA Read is an untagged request sent to the connection's Inbound RDMA Read Request Queue (IRRQ); the data comes back in tagged messages. Two numbers must be configured. The IRD (Inbound RDMA Read Queue Depth) is the size of the IRRQ. The ORD (Outbound RDMA Read Queue Depth) limits how many Read Requests a side may have outstanding, so that it never overruns the peer's IRRQ. The existing RDDP protocols leave both values to the ULP, so each ULP repeats the same logic for RDDP and InfiniBand.

The second problem is the missing Ready to Receive (RTR) indication. In MPA the active side never says that it has received the Reply, so that role is piggybacked on the first FULPDU the active side sends. That is a good optimization for client-server applications, but peer-to-peer ones, such as cluster calculations using MPI, cannot predict which node will have the first message to send.

The RFC explains why a dummy first message from the application is a poor workaround: it breaks transport-neutral APIs (only RDDP over TCP has a first-message requirement, unlike RDDP over SCTP and InfiniBand), it disturbs work queue and completion queue sizing, and it is awkward when MPA fencing is implemented in a host-based user-space library.
sections.eli5: Two kids sharing a toy box need to agree how many toys can be out at once. They also need someone to say "ready!" before play begins. The old rules made one kid always say it by doing something first, even with nothing to do.

sections.title: Enhanced MPA Request and Reply Frames
sections.content:
Enhanced setup keeps the MPA Request and Reply Frame layout but changes how the flag bits are used. A new S bit takes one bit from the old reserved Res field. It is one if the Private Data begins with the enhanced RDMA connection establishment data, and zero otherwise. With S at zero, the frames are identical to the unenhanced protocol. Because RFC 5044 says Res must be zero when sending and must not be checked on reception, the bit is backward compatible with the original frame format.

The Rev field must be two or higher to use any enhanced feature, and may be one if none is wanted. A host that accepts MPA connections MUST keep accepting version one requests even if it supports version two. PD_Length covers all Private Data, including the enhanced data when present.

For SCTP, three new function codes are added: Enhanced DDP Stream Session Initiate (0x005), Accept (0x006) and Reject (0x007). Private Data MUST be included in all three, and it MUST NOT exceed 512 bytes in any message, including the enhanced data. The Enhanced Reject code MUST be used for a configuration that would have been accepted in unenhanced negotiation.
sections.eli5: The old envelope had a spare box nobody used. The new rules tick that box to say "there is a special note at the start of my letter." Old readers ignore the tick, so the envelope still works.

sections.title: The Enhanced Connection Establishment Data
sections.content:
The enhanced data is a 32-bit block placed at the start of the Private Data, in network byte order. It holds the IRD and ORD as 14-bit unsigned integers and four control flags: A for the connection model, and B, C and D for the RTR indication type. ULP Private Data follows it, so the maximum ULP data shrinks by 4 bytes.

The initiator sends its IRD and ORD. The responder MUST set its ORD at most to the initiator's IRD, and may raise its IRD if the initiator's ORD is not enough. After the Accept, the initiator MUST set its IRD at least to the responder's ORD and its ORD at most to the responder's IRD. In short, initiator ORD is at most responder IRD, and responder ORD is at most initiator IRD. Both sides MUST pass the peer's values to the ULP. A side that lacks resources sends a TERM message with Layer 2, Error Type 0, Error Code 6.

The value 0x3FFF means automatic negotiation is not wanted and the ULP is responsible. The other side then leaves its own local value unchanged and echoes 0x3FFF in its reply.
sections.eli5: Each side says how many questions it can answer at once and how many it wants to ask. Then they pick numbers that fit, so nobody gets flooded.

sections.title: Peer-to-Peer Negotiation and the RTR Indication
sections.content:
Flag A set to 1 means a peer-to-peer connection, and 0 means client-server. When A is 1, flags B, C and D request or confirm the RTR indication type: a zero-length FULPDU (Send), a zero-length RDMA Write, or a zero-length RDMA Read. When A is 0, those three flags MUST be 0 and are ignored on reception.

The flow has three steps. The initiator's MPA Request sets A to 1, its IRD and ORD, and a flag for each RTR type it supports. The responder's MPA Reply echoes A, sets its actual IRD and ORD, and sets a flag for each RTR type it supports. The initiator then sends the first message using one of the negotiated types, chosen at its own discretion. The initiator MUST NOT send later FULPDUs before the RTR indication.

If the initiator cannot generate any of the responder's supported types, it MUST send a TERM message with Layer 2, Error Type 0, Error Code 7 and terminate the connection. The ULP may then negotiate a ULP-level RTR indication.
sections.eli5: The caller says which way it can say "I am ready": a wave, a nod or a thumbs up. The other side says which of those it understands, and the caller uses one that both know.

sections.title: Error Codes
sections.content:
Any enhanced setup error generates an MPA termination message. The layer and error type are 0x2 (LLP) and 0x0 (MPA). RFC 5044 defines four error codes and RFC 5043 defines none. This document adds three.

  • 0x05: Local catastrophic. Used for any local error that has no more specific code, before the connection is reset.
  • 0x06: Insufficient IRD resources.
  • 0x07: No matching RTR option.

IANA added these to the MPA Errors registry, and the three SCTP function codes to the registry for DDP session control, both created by RFC 6580.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong, a side sends a short numbered note: "I broke," "I do not have room," or "we have no way to say ready that we both know."

sections.title: Interoperability and Security
sections.content:
An initiator requests enhanced setup by sending an enhanced request. An enhanced responder MUST reply with an enhanced response. All responders MUST answer unenhanced requests with unenhanced responses, and MUST keep accepting unenhanced requests. An initiator MUST NOT use enhanced formats or function codes when it does not want enhanced functionality.

An unenhanced responder sees an enhanced request as incorrectly formatted and closes the TCP connection. Both sides then report the termination locally, and the initiator MAY retry with the unenhanced protocol if that suits the application, leaving ORD and IRD and peer-to-peer negotiation to the ULP.

On security, the RFC says the considerations from RFC 5044 and RFC 5043 apply and that these changes add no new ones. It recommends that implementations sanity-check the input parameters, including ORD, IRD and the control flags.
sections.eli5: If one side does not know the new rules, it hangs up. The caller can call back using the old rules. Everyone should still double-check numbers they are given.

messages.label: MPA Request
messages.note: Flag A is 1; initial IRD and ORD; flags B, C and D for each supported RTR type.

messages.label: MPA Reply
messages.note: Echoes A; actual IRD and ORD; flags for the RTR types it supports.

messages.label: First RDMA message (RTR)
messages.note: Uses a negotiated RTR type, or sends TERM if none matches.
